key_facts: Eczema caused by something touching the skin: **irritant (ICD, about 80%)** or **allergic (ACD, type IV delayed hypersensitivity)**.
Hands and face are the commonest sites; occupational exposure is frequent (hairdressers, healthcare, cleaners, builders).
ACD: about **25 allergens** cause half of cases; nickel is the leading cause worldwide.
Identify and avoid the cause (**patch testing** for suspected ACD), emollients and soap substitutes, topical steroid.
Persistent occupational dermatitis may need specialist and occupational health input.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: **Contact dermatitis** is eczema caused by something touching the skin. **Irritant contact dermatitis (ICD)** is commoner and dose-dependent. **Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD)** needs prior sensitisation and is confirmed by **patch testing**.

Atopic eczema pathways and general steroid/emollient skills sit on [eczema / dermatitis](condition:eczema-dermatitis). This page deepens ICD vs ACD, occupational disease, cosmetics, tattoos and patch-testing referral.

sub: Contact dermatitis accounts for most **occupational skin disease**; irritant contact dermatitis is about four times commoner than allergic.
Any age; more common in adults with wet work; atopic people are at higher risk of irritant dermatitis.
Nickel allergy is commonest in women (jewellery, piercings) but falling in Europe since the EU Nickel Directive.

head: ICD
ACD
rows: Tiny amounts can elicit once sensitised

ul: Common irritants: water, detergents, solvents, cutting oils, friction, heat.
Common allergens: nickel, fragrance mixes, rubber accelerators, preservatives (MI/MCI), PPD hair dye, topical antibiotics/steroids, epoxy resins.
Mixed ICD+ACD is frequent on hands. About four-fifths of occupational hand dermatitis starts as irritant.
**Irritants**: water and wet work, soaps and detergents, solvents, friction, cutting oils, alkalis and acids.

**Common allergens**: nickel, cobalt, chromate (cement, leather), fragrances, preservatives (**methylisothiazolinone**, formaldehyde releasers), **PPD** hair dye, rubber accelerators, topical medicines (neomycin, corticosteroids), plants (*Primula*, Compositae).
A damaged barrier (e.g. atopic eczema, leg ulcers, perianal disease) increases sensitisation to topical medicines.
**"I've used it for years, so I can't be allergic"**: sensitisation can develop after years of exposure.
**"Hypoallergenic products are safe"**: they can still contain relevant allergens.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: **Irritant** dermatitis is direct damage; **allergic** dermatitis is a learned T-cell response.

mech.t: Irritants strip lipids and damage keratinocytes directly, causing barrier loss and non-specific inflammation in anyone exposed enough; no prior sensitisation needed.
mech.caption: Irritant dermatitis (direct damage) vs allergic dermatitis (sensitised T cells).

mech.t: Small reactive chemicals (**haptens**, under 500 Da) bind skin proteins; Langerhans cells carry them to lymph nodes and prime specific **T cells** (10–15 days).
mech.caption: Sensitisation: a small chemical (hapten) binds skin protein; a Langerhans cell carries it to the lymph node, where specific T cells multiply.

mech.t: On re-exposure, memory T cells release cytokines at the contact site within **24–72 hours**, causing eczema (type IV hypersensitivity).
Eczema can spread beyond the contact area (autosensitisation); continued exposure leads to chronic, lichenified, fissured dermatitis.

histo: Spongiotic dermatitis (intercellular oedema, vesicles) with lymphocytes; eosinophils favour allergic dermatitis.
Irritant: keratinocyte necrosis and neutrophils in acute damage. Histology cannot identify the cause: **patch testing** does.

ul: Both look eczematous: erythema, vesicles, scale, fissures, lichenification.
ICD: burning/stinging often > itch; sharp borders early; interdigital “sentinel” wet-work dermatitis.
ACD: itch dominates; geometric patterns (glove, plaster, jewellery); may spread beyond contact.
Facial/cosmetic ACD: eyelids, hairline; airborne fragrance can affect exposed face.
Tattoo ink allergy: localised eczema or lichenoid reaction in a colour distribution.
Skin of colour: erythema less obvious; violaceous pigment and lichenification more prominent.

bodymap.caption: Classic allergic contact sites: eyelids (nail varnish, cosmetics), earlobes (nickel), wrist (watch strap), below the navel (jeans stud), hands (gloves, products).
pts: **Face, eyelids and neck** (cosmetics, airborne allergens, nail varnish).

ul: History: occupation, hobbies, cosmetics, topical medicines, holiday improvement.
ICD: clinical exposure story; no confirmatory lab test.
Suspected ACD that is chronic, recurrent, occupational, facial or treatment-resistant → **refer for patch testing** (British baseline ± relevant series + patient’s own products).
Photopatch testing when sunscreen filters or photoallergens are suspected.
Prick testing / specific IgE is for immediate contact urticaria (e.g. latex), not delayed ACD.

ol: Identify and **avoid** the irritant/allergen — improvement can take weeks.
Soap substitute + liberal emollient; cotton liners under gloves for wet work.
Short topical corticosteroid matched to site and severity (face/flexures: mild–moderate).
Refer for patch testing when indicated (CKS/BAD/PCDS).
Occupational cases: fit-note/workplace adjustments; RIDDOR awareness is employer-led — IPs recognise and signpost.

blocks.title: Emollient cautions
blocks.text: Do not use aqueous cream as a leave-on. Counsel paraffin fire risk and slippery bathroom floors.

blocks.title: Pigmented contact dermatitis
blocks.text: Grey-brown facial pigment from cosmetics/fragrances in darker skin — see [contact & lichenoid pigmentation](condition:contact-lichenoid-pigmentation).

ladder.t: Identify and **avoid** the irritant or allergen. Soap substitute + liberal emollient.
**Short topical corticosteroid** matched to site and severity. Face and flexures: mild to moderate potency.
Refer for **patch testing** when indicated (CKS / BAD / PCDS).
Fit note and workplace adjustments. RIDDOR reporting is employer-led: recognise and signpost.

blocks.title: Prescribing limits and pitfalls
list: **Aqueous cream**: Not as a leave-on emollient.
**Paraffin emollients**: Fire risk on fabrics; slippery floors.
**Facial pigment**: Grey-brown pigment from cosmetics in darker skin: see contact & lichenoid pigmentation.

refer.t: Severe **facial or eyelid swelling**, or systemic contact dermatitis.
**Occupational** disease threatening livelihood: early patch testing and workplace advice.
Suspected **airborne** allergy continuing despite stopping perfume.
Not healing on treatment: think allergy to the **medicament** itself.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Occupational disease threatening livelihood — early patch testing and workplace advice.
Severe facial/eyelid swelling or systemic contact dermatitis.
Suspected airborne allergy continuing despite “stopping perfume”.
Non-healing dermatitis on medicaments — think contact allergy to the treatment itself.
Chronic hand dermatitis with loss of work; secondary bacterial infection.
Severe facial and scalp swelling after PPD hair dye.
Spread (autosensitisation) and erythroderma (rare).
ICD improves when exposure stops, but barrier recovery takes weeks to months.
ACD is lifelong: avoidance prevents recurrence; occupational ACD can persist even after avoidance.

pearls: Many “allergies” on the hands are **irritant** — still treat the barrier aggressively.
Atopics get ICD more easily and can still develop ACD.
Hair-dye (PPD) and nail-varnish eyelid patterns are classic teaching cases.
Always check BNF/SmPC for topical steroid site limits.

quiz.q: Irritant or allergic: which needs prior sensitisation?
quiz.a: Allergic contact dermatitis (type IV). Irritant needs no sensitisation and is dose-dependent.

quiz.q: When does allergic contact dermatitis appear after re-exposure?
Which test confirms allergic contact dermatitis?
quiz.a: Patch testing (prick tests / IgE are for immediate contact urticaria).

quiz.q: Who should be referred for patch testing?
quiz.a: Chronic, recurrent, occupational, facial or treatment-resistant suspected allergic contact dermatitis.

quiz.q: A rash worsens under a cream you prescribed. Think?
quiz.a: Contact allergy to the medicament itself (e.g. topical antibiotic or steroid).
